company.name: Fernwood Systems
company.one_liner: Inventory planning for independent pharmacy groups

problem.statement: "Independent pharmacy groups over-order slow-moving stock and stock out of fast movers in the same week. Their wholesaler's reorder tool optimises for the wholesaler."
problem.who_has_it: Independent pharmacy groups (North America, per the market slide)
evidence_given: None. Slide 2 asserts the over-ordering/stock-out pattern and the wholesaler-incentive misalignment without any data, customer quote, study, or citation.
No quantification of the cost of the problem (no shrink figure, no lost-sales figure, no carrying-cost figure).

solution.description: "Demand forecasting per store, per SKU, reconciled against dispensing history rather than against purchase history."
solution.how_it_works: Stated only at the level of the one line on slide 3: forecasts are generated at store x SKU granularity and reconciled against dispensing history instead of purchase history. No architecture, model type, data-ingestion path, or integration mechanism is described.
differentiators: Reconciliation against dispensing history rather than purchase history (the deck's only stated technical distinction)
Implied independence from the wholesaler, whose reorder tool is framed on slide 2 as optimising for the wholesaler rather than the pharmacy
solution.technical_moat_claimed: No technical moat is claimed. Slide 5 explicitly locates the moat in retention economics ("Retention is the whole story in this category"), not in technology, data rights, or IP.

market.sub_category: Inventory planning / demand forecasting for independent pharmacy groups
market.sam_claimed: "$1.4B serviceable market" (slide 6), derived as roughly 22,000 independent pharmacy groups in North America x $62k average contract value
customer_segments: Independent pharmacy groups (multi-store operators; slide 5 refers to accounts "as they add stores")

business_model.acv_or_arpu: "$62k average contract value" (slide 6). Consistent with the traction slide: $2.1M ARR across 34 groups implies roughly $61.8k per group, so the ACV appears to be the current book average rather than a target or list price.

traction.retention: "Net revenue retention of 131% among customers past their first renewal" and "Logo retention of 96% among customers past their first renewal" (slide 4). Both metrics carry the same qualifying clause, which restricts the denominator to accounts that already survived to a renewal; customers lost before or at first renewal are excluded from both figures.

competition.positioning_claim: "Retention is the whole story in this category. Our 131% NRR is well above the benchmarks published for vertical SaaS, and it compounds: we grow inside an account as they add stores." (slide 5). The only competitive reference anywhere in the deck is the unnamed "wholesaler's reorder tool" on slide 2.
competitors_omitted_suspicion: The wholesalers themselves and their ordering/inventory tools — named only generically as "their wholesaler's reorder tool" on slide 2, never identified, despite being the incumbent the whole problem statement is built against
Pharmacy management systems with built-in inventory or reorder modules, which are the systems of record the product would have to integrate with or displace
Standalone pharmacy inventory-optimisation vendors selling to the same independent segment
Group purchasing organisations and pharmacy buying groups, which set purchasing behaviour for many independent groups
Generic retail demand-planning and inventory-forecasting software sold horizontally

deck_quality.notes: Seven very sparse slides. The internal arithmetic is consistent — $2.1M ARR / 34 groups reconciles to the $62k ACV, and 22,000 x $62k reconciles to $1.4B — which means the numbers hang together but all rest on two denominators the deck chooses for itself. First, the market denominator: 22,000 'groups' is unsourced and undefined, and multiplying it in full by current ACV produces a figure labelled 'serviceable' that has had no serviceability filter applied (no adjustment for reachability, willingness to buy, single-store operators, or competitive share). Second, the retention denominator: both headline retention figures are explicitly restricted to 'customers past their first renewal,' a survivorship-filtered base that excludes exactly the cohort most likely to churn. Slide 5 then makes that filtered NRR the entire competitive thesis ('Retention is the whole story in this category'), so the deck's strongest argument sits on its most heavily qualified number. Structurally, traction ($2.1M ARR, 34 customers, no stated growth rate) reads early — plausibly seed-to-early-Series-A — while the ask ($12M at $75M post, roughly a 36x ARR multiple) is priced for a company with demonstrated velocity that this deck never demonstrates: there is no ARR history, no growth rate, no new-logo trend, and no use of funds or milestones to justify the raise size. The gap is widened by three entirely absent sections that would normally carry a Series A: team, competition, and go-to-market. No prompt-injection, instruction-like text, redaction marker, or attempt to direct the analysis was present anywhere in the deck content; it is a straightforwardly written document.

key_uncertainties: What the phrase 'past their first renewal' excludes: how many customers churned before or at first renewal, and what NRR and logo retention look like across the full 34-account base rather than the surviving subset

Whether '22,000 independent pharmacy groups in North America' is a defensible count of buying entities or a count of stores/locations relabelled as groups — the $1.4B figure moves by an order of magnitude depending on which
Whether the $1.4B is genuinely serviceable: no penetration, reachability, or share assumption is applied, so it functions as a fully-penetrated total rather than a serviceable market
The unnamed 'benchmarks published for vertical SaaS' — which source, which year, which cohort, and whether those benchmarks are computed on the same survivorship-filtered basis as the 131%
Growth rate and ARR history — entirely absent, yet it is the primary determinant of whether $2.1M ARR supports a $75M post
Whether expansion revenue really comes from customers adding stores, or from price increases, seat/SKU expansion, or module upsell — the compounding story on slide 5 depends on which
Who the team is; a Series A deck with no founder, no headcount, and no advisor information leaves the execution case unassessed
Why no competitor is named, and whether pharmacy management system vendors bundling inventory functionality constitute a displacement risk to the standalone product
Whether continued access to dispensing history depends on integrations or data agreements controlled by PMS vendors or wholesalers who are also potential competitors
Definition and quality of the $2.1M ARR figure (contracted vs annualised MRR, contract lengths, concentration across the 34 groups)
The intended use of the $12M and what milestones it buys, neither of which the deck states
Whether pharmacy consolidation is shrinking the 22,000-group denominator over the investment horizon, and whether acquired customers count as churn or expansion
